docs.title: Vergil
docs.text:
Vergil is a fleet-management and repository-governance system: a Python toolchain (vergil-tooling), a Claude Code behavioral plugin, reusable CI/CD actions, and isolated container/VM environments — all coordinated by a two-tier epic / task planning model.

This site is the project's home: what Vergil is, where it's going, and what's shipped recently.

docs.title: Where the project is going
docs.text: The Roadmap is generated from the open epics across every repo in the organization — one view of every cross-cutting initiative, refreshed automatically.

docs.title: What's shipping
docs.text: The Activity log is the by-date record of recently closed work across the whole org.

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text: Vergil validates repositories across a set of first-class, containerized, multi-version languages — Python, Go, Java, Rust, C++, and now TypeScript (Node.js runtime, single canonical tsc, npm, Vitest + V8 100% coverage, a shareable strict base tsconfig, node-24 / node-22 images). See Supported languages for the fleet-level summary.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Every repository in the fleet runs the same CI model, and it is version-agnostic by design: the set of language versions a repo tests against is configuration, not workflow code, and the merge gates never name a version. The versions come from a fleet-wide version window, so a new or dropped language version reaches every repo without an edit; nothing about the workflows or the branch protection has to move with it.

This page is the fleet-level summary. The authoritative mechanics — job names, the reusable-workflow inputs, the evidence bundle format — live in vergil-tooling and are linked below rather than restated here:

  • CI Architecture
  • CI Evidence Convention

docs.title: The version set comes from the version window
docs.text:
A repo's CI version matrix is not embedded in ci.yml and not passed as a workflow input. It comes from the version window, the set of language versions Vergil supports, through one chain:

  1. The manifest. vergil-containers records each language's window in docker/versions/manifest.yml. Every version list in that repo is generated from it.
  2. The published window. The generator also writes docker/versions/window.json, which consumers read at the v2.1 ref.
  3. The resolver. vrg-ci-resolve, in vergil-tooling, reads the window and the repo's vergil.toml and returns the versions to build. Every CI run uses it, through the vergil-actions CI setup, and so does local validation. The matrix fans out over what it returns — a dynamic matrix.

What the resolver returns depends on the repo:

  • No pin. With no [ci].versions, a repo follows the window. A library ([project].repository-type) builds every version in the window. Any other repository type is an app, and builds one version: the newest.
  • [ci].versions is an optional pin. A pinned version that is not in the window is a fatal error, and so is an app pin with more than one version. A pin is visible technical debt, not the normal way to choose versions.

The window moves on its own. A nightly lifecycle job in vergil-containers compares each language's window with its upstream's release and end-of-life data, and opens the add, drop and runtime pull requests that change it (see Nightly governance). A repo that does not pin picks up the change on its next run, with no edit of its own, and no ci.yml is hand-edited, so the matrix cannot drift from the window.

The window, the pin rules and the lifecycle rules are documented once, in vergil-containers' Language version lifecycle page.

docs.title: Thin-caller ci.yml
docs.text:
A consuming repo's ci.yml is a thin caller. Each job simply uses: a vergil-actions reusable workflow at the pinned @v2.1 tag and passes only language: and container-suffix:. It passes no version matrix and no container tag — both resolve dynamically: the matrix from the version window (or from the [ci].versions pin, if one is set), and the single-container jobs' image tag from the primary version (below).

Because the matrix and the container tag are derived rather than written down, the same short workflow serves every repo, and a version change takes effect fleet-wide without touching a single ci.yml.

One exception to "pass only language: and container-suffix:": a repo that publishes packages (see Release packaging) must call the release workflow with secrets: inherit. Its signing secrets are environment secrets, and an explicit secrets: map does not deliver environment secrets to a cross-repo reusable workflow — only inherit does. Semgrep flags secrets: inherit, so the line carries an inline suppression:

    secrets: inherit  # nosemgrep: yaml.github-actions.security.secrets-inherit.secrets-inherit

docs.title: Version-agnostic evidence gates
docs.text:
Branch protection requires stable, version-agnostic aggregate checks, not per-version legs. For each matrixed kind — audit, quality, and tests — the required check is the <kind> / evidence aggregate the reusable workflow emits (audit / evidence, quality / evidence, test / evidence), never the individual … / 3.12, … / 3.13 legs. Each evidence job depends on the whole matrix, so one required context covers every version.

quality / evidence also covers the quality workflow's two single-container jobs: it aggregates quality / common (the common checks), quality / custom (the repo's custom validator), and the matrixed lint and typecheck legs. It runs even when one of them fails, so any failure fails the gate. It is required in every repo's CI-gates ruleset, whatever the language; quality / common is no longer required on its own.

The custom validator (scripts/bin/validate-custom) therefore runs in PR CI as well as in local vrg-validate, and a failing validator blocks the merge. A repo with no custom validator gets a passing no-op quality / custom job.

Because the required-check names carry no version, a matrix change merges through the normal gate — including a matrix reduction. This closes the old deadlock, where branch protection required a per-version leg that a reduced matrix could never produce, leaving the PR "expected, never reported" and permanently blocked with no --admin escape. A version change is now an ordinary PR.

The non-matrixed checks (the security scanners, the version-bump gate, the docs build) keep their fixed, version-free names, and they are required too — there are no report-only PR gates.

docs.title: [ci].primary-version for single-container jobs
docs.text: Some jobs are not matrixed — they run once in a single container (for example the security scan, the version-bump gate, and the docs build). These run on the primary version: [ci].primary-version if it is set, otherwise the newest resolved version (for Python, 3.15 today). primary-version is the escape hatch for the rare case where the newest version is not the right single-container default.

docs.title: Release packaging
docs.text:
A repo whose vergil.toml has a [package] table also builds signed .deb / .rpm packages and publishes them to the org's package repository. Three vergil-actions reusable workflows carry it; repos without [package] call none of the packaging jobs and see no change.

  • ci-package.yml (PR CI). Builds every package and install-tests it in a clean container of each target OS, rolling up into the single package / evidence gate. It runs one of two tiers: full (every build cell and every test cell) for release PRs into main and non-PR events, and reduced (every build cell, but only one test cell per format — the oldest release, on amd64) for other feature PRs.
  • cd-release.yml (release). package-matrix resolves the cells, package-build builds them unsigned, and package-sign — in the main-only package-signing environment — signs every .rpm and attests every artifact. The release job then attaches the signed packages and packages-manifest.json to the GitHub Release and dispatches to packages. Any packaging failure stops the release before it is tagged.
  • publish-index.yml (the packages repo). Rebuilds the apt and dnf index from the product releases. Before indexing anything it verifies every asset's build attestation, pinned to cd-release.yml on refs/heads/main, and every .rpm's signature, then signs the metadata in the develop-only index-signing environment and deploys to GitHub Pages.

The release caller needs secrets: inherit (see Thin-caller ci.yml). The full mechanics are in vergil-tooling's CI Architecture guide and the Package Config Reference.

docs.title: Nightly governance (ops.yml)
docs.text:
Checking this model across the fleet is itself automated. Every managed repo carries an ops.yml workflow that calls the vergil-actions reusable workflow ops-github-config.yml on a nightly schedule. A repo whose ops.yml is missing or has no schedule is treated as non-compliant. The nightly run has three jobs:

  • Config audit. vrg-github-repo-config audit compares the repo's GitHub configuration and its checked-in files against the canonical Vergil configuration. It reports drift, such as branch protection that does not match the derived required-check set or a required context that no workflow can produce, and any drift fails the run. The nightly job only audits; it never changes the configuration. Reconciling a repo (apply) is a human action. See the GitHub Config Audit reference.
  • Dependabot audit. vrg-dependabot-audit fails the run when the repo has any open Dependabot alert, described below.
  • Branch sweep. vrg-branch-sweep deletes branches whose pull-request work is finished. It is the safety net behind the delete-on-merge and delete-on-close rules. See the vrg-branch-sweep reference.

The nightly ops.yml in vergil-containers also runs the language lifecycle job, which keeps the version window current. For Python and Go it opens one pull request per change: an add, a drop, or (for Python) a runtime change that records a newly published vergil-python runtime. For the other languages it opens an issue instead. It never enables auto-merge: a person reviews and merges every lifecycle pull request.

docs.title: Report-only Dependabot
docs.text:
Dependabot alerts are on for every repo, and Dependabot never opens a pull request. The config audit enforces both settings: alerts on, Dependabot security updates off. Every repo also carries a canonical .github/dependabot.yml in which every entry sets open-pull-requests-limit: 0. vrg-validate rejects an entry without that limit, and the config audit flags a missing or non-canonical file. The file exists so that the OpenSSF Scorecard Dependency-Update-Tool check passes.

The nightly dependabot-audit job fails on any open alert, at any severity. vrg-dependabot-audit exits 1 when the repo has open alerts and 2 when it could not check them, and both fail the run. The log of a public repo shows alert counts only. The only way to clear an alert is to fix the dependency or dismiss the alert on GitHub; nothing in the repo can suppress one.

This gate is defense in depth, aimed at dormant repos. The dependency update at release time and the language audits that run on every change remain the main dependency hygiene. See the Dependabot Alert Audit reference.

docs.title: Python toolchain selection
docs.text:
Vergil owns which Python interpreter runs. A repo's own files may declare only a floor, such as requires-python:

  • .python-version is an error. It chooses the interpreter version behind Vergil's back, so validation fails until it is deleted.
  • uv's python-preference and python-downloads are allowed. They choose where an interpreter comes from, not which version it is.
  • Vergil sets the interpreter itself. Wherever it runs Python, it sets UV_PYTHON to the resolved version and UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE=only-system, so uv always uses the image's interpreter.

See rule 13 of the Language version lifecycle and vergil-tooling's Container Config Reference.

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text:
Vergil supports a set of first-class languages under one shared model: containerized, multi-version toolchains with a common validation pipeline (lint, typecheck, test + coverage, dependency audit). Each language is added the same way — a registry entry, a strictness policy, prebuilt container images, and reusable CI — so every repository is validated identically regardless of the language it is written in. Each language's versions come from its version window, published by vergil-containers and derived from the upstream community's release and end-of-life policy, not from workflow code; see vergil-containers' Language version lifecycle for the per-language policies, and Continuous integration for the fleet-wide, version-agnostic CI model.

This page is the fleet-level summary. The authoritative, per-language standards (toolchains, strictness rules, naming, testing and coverage) live in vergil-tooling and are linked below rather than restated here.

Language Standards Python Python standards Go Go standards Java Java standards Rust Rust standards C++ C++ standards TypeScript (new) TypeScript standards

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text:
TypeScript is the newest first-class language, and the first new language added since the extension model matured with C++. It follows the same containerized, multi-version pattern as the rest of the fleet. The v1 shape:

  • Node.js runtime, single canonical tsc. TypeScript has no Clang-vs-GCC analog — there is exactly one typechecker. So TYPECHECK, LINT, and AUDIT each run once, and only the test stage fans out per Node major. That makes the expensive matrix axis the Node version, not the compiler — and makes TypeScript lighter on merge gates than C++.
  • Multi-version container images. The toolchain ships as prebuilt stable images for the supported Node majors — node-24 (primary) and node-22 — never built from source.
  • npm for install and audit. Install is npm ci (a clean, lockfile-pinned install from package-lock.json); the dependency audit is npm audit. npm was chosen for universality at zero adoption barrier.
  • Warnings to 11, via a shareable strict base tsconfig. Strictness is the baseline, not a luxury: consumers extend a shared strict base tsconfig (strict plus a curated set of extras promoted to errors), so every repository typechecks clean against the same rules.
  • 100% coverage with Vitest + V8. The house line is held at 100% via Vitest's V8 coverage, with explicit /* v8 ignore */ markers as the acknowledged-gap valve — gaps are declared, never silently dropped.
  • ESM-first. v1 targets native ES modules (nodenext resolution, es2022 target); CommonJS and plain untyped JavaScript are out of scope for v1.

For the full toolchain, strictness rules, and testing policy, see the TypeScript standards in vergil-tooling:

  • Toolchain and strictness
  • Testing and coverage
  • Naming conventions

docs.title: Package repository
docs.text: Vergil products are published as signed OS packages — .deb for Ubuntu and .rpm for RHEL — through one org-wide package repository. This page is the fleet-level summary. The full install commands live in the packages README, and the build side lives in vergil-tooling's Package Config Reference and CI Architecture guide.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
The repository is served from GitHub Pages at https://vergil-project.github.io/packages:

Format Path Releases apt /deb Ubuntu 24.04 (noble), Ubuntu 26.04 (resolute) rpm /rpm/el9, /rpm/el10 RHEL 9, RHEL 10

Every release is published for both amd64 and arm64. The indexed products today are vergil-tooling, vergil-python (the pinned CPython runtime the Python products run on), and vergil-archive-keyring (built by the packages repo itself).

docs.title: Bootstrapping a host
docs.text:
A host trusts the repository in four steps:

  1. Fetch the public key from keys/vergil.asc on the repository site.
  2. Verify that it holds exactly one primary key, with fingerprint B3A1D804DC03AB036566A4E367861822166ECABE.
  3. Add a temporary bootstrap source signed by that key and install vergil-archive-keyring. From then on the keyring package owns the key and the permanent apt source / dnf repo file.
  4. Remove the bootstrap source and key.

The exact apt and dnf commands are in the packages README and are not repeated here. On a vergil-managed VM, vrg-package performs this bootstrap itself and refuses any key whose primary fingerprint differs from the pinned one.

docs.title: Signing model
docs.text:
The org has one OpenPGP identity. Its primary key is RSA-4096, certify-only, and held offline by a human. CI never sees it. CI holds only a signing subkey, which signs every .rpm and the apt (InRelease / Release.gpg) and dnf (repomd.xml) metadata.

Trust the primary fingerprint, not the subkey. The subkey rotates: a new one is minted offline and shipped as a new vergil-archive-keyring release, so a host that trusts the primary picks it up through an ordinary upgrade.

The subkey lives in GitHub environments restricted by branch: package-signing (admits only main) in each product repo, where a release signs its packages, and index-signing (admits only develop) in packages, where the index is signed. Sigstore build-provenance attestations are an extra layer on top of the signatures, never the trust root.

docs.title: Who installs which way
docs.text:
Environment How vergil-tooling is installed Agent VMs (Lima and cloud) From the package repository, with apt Dev containers uv tool install (the container cache) macOS host uv tool install

On a VM, vrg-vm pins vergil-tooling to the identity's resolved version and fails provisioning if the repository has no matching package; it never falls back to a uv install. See vergil-tooling's VM spec reference.

Packaged Python products depend on the vergil-python runtime series they were built against. vergil-python publishes one package per listed CPython series, vergil-python<x.y>, and every release publishes every listed series. A package's version is <cpython>+<pbs_tag>.<release>, where <release> is the vergil-python release that built it (for example 3.15.1+20261021.1.0.4); releases before v1.0.4 lack the .<release> suffix. A product depends on vergil-python<x.y> (>= <installed version>), the runtime version it was built against, so later patches and rebuilds of the same series satisfy it.

The series is derived: it is the newest window version with a published runtime. A product can instead pin an exact x.y.z with [package.python] runtime, and then the build fails if the series package serves any other patch. For a pinned product, the vergil updater in vrg-update-deps bumps the pin to the patch the series package serves, only once every package index the build and install-test read from serves it, and never outside the pin's series: a newer series is reported as held back. See vergil-tooling's Package Config Reference and Dependency Update Config.

docs.title: Publishing a product
docs.text: A repo opts in by adding a [package] table to its vergil.toml (builder, vendor, summary, smoke test, and target selection). With it present, PR CI builds and install-tests the packages, and a release builds, signs, attests and attaches them to the GitHub Release, then notifies packages to re-index. Without it, nothing changes. The keys are documented in the Package Config Reference; the pipeline is summarized under Release packaging.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Vergil's Management layer is how work is organized and moved — from a raw idea to a merged, closed change — across every repository and org in the fleet. It is one of several Vergil frameworks (alongside Security, Testing, and the VM/identity and container layers); this one owns the work itself: what we are doing, why, in what order, and how it gets done.

It is deliberately two-directional. Looking down, it lets you manage and zoom into the smallest unit — a single task, one pull request. Looking up, it lets you zoom out to the strategic view — every cross-cutting initiative in flight, across the whole organization, in one place. The same model serves both, and the point is to keep climbing: once you can manage tasks, you manage epics; once you can manage epics, you manage how epics interrelate.

docs.title: Units of work and delivery
docs.text:
Two definitions do the load-bearing work here:

  • The unit of work is the task — an issue that represents a single task, implemented by a single pull request and closed the moment that PR merges. This one-issue-to-one-PR discipline is exactly what makes the trailing end of the process — closing and roll-up — automatable.
  • The unit of delivery is the epic — a collection of related tasks that together implement a larger, more complex body of functionality. You deliver epics; the tasks are the to-dos that implement them.

Historically the unit was the issue: have an idea, file an issue, go do it. That broke down — a single issue was often complex enough to need many pull requests, sometimes across repositories. Splitting work from delivery fixes it: the task is small and mechanical, the epic is the meaningful whole.

docs.title: Three invariants
docs.text:
Everything in this layer follows from three rules:

  1. Every issue belongs to an epic. An issue is either an epic (or one of the bookkeeping kinds: a per-quarter archive bucket, a release tracking issue) or it has an epic parent. There is no "unlinked" state — even a one-line idea is captured under the intake epic — and the parent is the issue's state: intake, planning, deferred, or ready to build.
  2. All epics live in the organization's .github repository — one place to see every initiative in the org. (A private repository keeps its own, so private work never surfaces in public.)
  3. Every other repository holds nothing but single-PR tasks — each closed by exactly one pull request in that same repository.

The load-bearing principle behind the third rule is task↔PR locality: a task lives in the repository whose pull request closes it. Cohesion between a task and the change that completes it matters more than a pristine issue list. In practice the .github list reads as "epics, and the issues linked under them" — you filter by the epic label for the initiatives — and the items that live there (queue items under the intake, planning and deferred epics, and the rare task whose PR edits .github itself) are linked like everything else.

docs.title: The shape of the model
docs.text:
• Epics & tasks — finite epics (in .github), plus one perpetual ad-hoc epic per repository for the small, unplanned work that should never accrete into a larger initiative.
  • Intake, planning & deferred — three standing queues that catch raw input the moment it occurs and hold it until it is ready: work flows intake → planning → ready, an evaluated item that cannot move yet waits in deferred with the conditions that will bring it back, and only ready work can be built, so nothing is lost before it is planned.
  • Workflow — how an idea becomes an epic becomes shipped tasks: the epic-create orchestrator and a front-loaded design pipeline with human-gated review rounds that makes implementation near-bulletproof.
  • Tools & skills — how the vrg-* commands and the skills fit together: what each does at the story level, and which are driven by a human versus an agent. The per-command reference lives in the repositories where the code does.

One convention is worth stating up front, because it shapes the whole lifecycle: an epic opens with a documentation task and does not close until you have reviewed it, decided what comes next, and confirmed the docs reflect what changed. Nothing is ever "done" without asking what comes next.

docs.title: Epics & tasks
docs.text: The model has exactly two artifacts — the task (the unit of work) and the epic (the unit of delivery) — plus a family of perpetual standing epics for the work that is not (or not yet) part of a plan.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A task is an issue that represents a single, self-contained change:

  • It is implemented by exactly one pull request, in the repository where that PR lands (task↔PR locality).
  • It is born linked to an epic — as is every issue: see Every issue belongs to an epic. On GitHub the link is a native sub-issue; on forges without sub-issues it degrades to a portable Parent: <owner>/<repo>#<n> line in the task body. Either way, the tooling speaks one vocabulary and never the underlying mechanism.
  • It closes when its PR merges. A task with an epic parent links its PR with the Closes keyword, so the merge closes the task automatically; the one close keyword is Closes (Fixes/Resolves are banned to keep it unambiguous).

Because a task is exactly one PR, "done" is unambiguous: once the change is in the trunk, the task is finished. Any later change is a new task, never a reopening.

docs.title: Finite epics
docs.text:
A finite epic is a cross-cutting initiative with an end — a real project made of related tasks, often spanning several repositories. It carries the epic label and lives in the org's .github. Its spec and plan live beside it, at epics/<n>-<slug>/ in .github.

When every child task of a finite epic is closed, the epic rolls up — it auto-closes. Roll-up is event-driven: an on: issues.closed Action fires the check on every issue close, so an epic wraps itself up the moment its last task lands, with no human bookkeeping.

docs.title: Ad-hoc epics
docs.text:
Not all work belongs to an initiative. The small, unplanned, standalone things — fix a typo in a man page, bump a pin — would clutter the model if each demanded its own epic. So every repository has exactly one ad-hoc epic: Epic (ad hoc): <repo>, labelled epic + ad-hoc, and (like all epics) located in .github. Its tasks live in the target repository, linked across.

ad-hoc is the single marker for this perpetual variant. An earlier standing alias has been retired — removed from the code and the label registry — so ad-hoc is the only form the model recognises.

An ad-hoc epic is perpetual: created once, never auto-closed, kept open even when empty. That perpetual-ness is the only thing distinguishing it from a finite epic. The name does deliberate work — "ad hoc" is the smell a serious engineer drives toward zero. The long-term goal is for ad-hoc work to become the rare exception as real work is increasingly shaped into finite, tidy, self-closing epics.

As its children close they drain into per-quarter archive buckets, so the live ad-hoc epic shows only work still in flight.

docs.title: Standing epics
docs.text:
The ad-hoc epic is one of four standing epics — perpetual umbrellas that are created once, reused, and never roll up:

Standing epic Holds Epic (ad hoc): <repo> ready one-off work for one repository Epic (intake): <name> captured, unreviewed items — and every orphan the sweep finds Epic (planning): <name> items waiting for (or undergoing) epic creation Epic (deferred): <name> evaluated items parked until their revival conditions are met

There is one ad-hoc epic per repository. The intake, planning and deferred epics come as a set per queue home: the org's .github for every public repository, and the repository itself for a private one. They are the three queues that hold work before it is ready to build — see Intake, planning & deferred.

docs.title: Every issue belongs to an epic
docs.text:
In any managed repository, every issue is either a legitimate top-level kind or has an epic parent. The top-level kinds are epics (including the standing ones), the per-quarter archive buckets, and the release tracking issue a release opens for its duration. Everything else — tasks, operational tasks, intake, planning and deferred items — hangs under an epic.

There is no opt-out and no "unlinked" state, and the parent is not just bookkeeping: it is the issue's state. Under the intake epic it has been captured; under the planning epic it awaits a design; under the deferred epic it waits for its revival conditions; under an ad-hoc or finite epic it is ready to build. The sanctioned tools create every issue already linked, and an issue born outside them is healed, not rejected — the daily sweep attaches it to its home's intake epic.

docs.title: The bookend convention
docs.text:
An epic is never truly "done" the instant its implementation lands, because almost no real problem is 100% closed by a single initiative. So every epic carries bookend tasks:

  • It opens with a documentation task — the spec and plan, born from planning.
  • It closes with two tasks, in order: a documentation review (confirm the change is reflected in the docs — especially this site) and then the retrospective, the terminal gate — a single backward-looking record that partners the spec and plan and records what comes next. Its docs PR closes the epic.
  • A follow-on brainstorm is seeded up front only when a known follow-on already exists; otherwise its outcome is captured in the retrospective.

This rides the roll-up: because the epic cannot close until all its tasks close, the closing bookends gate completion. You cannot finish an epic without answering "now what?" and confirming the story is documented. Nothing is ever done without asking what comes next.

docs.title: Compliance invariants
docs.text:
These guarantees are enforced, not just documented. vrg-epic-audit is a read-only sweep (with a human-gated --close) that flags drift and invariant violations:

  • Epics live in .github. A public repository's epics belong in the org's .github; an epic that has leaked out is flagged. (A private repository may legitimately home its own epics.)
  • No stray .github issues. The epic home holds only epics, the per-quarter archive buckets, and issues linked under an epic — tasks and intake, planning and deferred queue items alike. Any other open issue there is a stray.
  • An epic is never closed while a child is open. Roll-up closes a finite epic only once all its children are closed; a closed epic with a still-open child is a violation, remediated by reopening it. (Standing epics never roll up; their closed children drain into archives instead.)
  • Every issue has an epic parent. An orphan — an open issue that is neither a top-level kind nor linked under an epic — is reported, along with any issue still carrying the retired triage / idea / research labels.
  • No private work under public epics. Visibility changes are supported in one direction only. Private → public is supported: the sweep moves the repository's queue items under the org's .github queues, and its epics are relocated. Public → private is unsupported — create a new private repository and migrate the code instead. A private repository's issue found under a public .github epic is reported for a human to resolve.

The daily sweep (vrg-epic-audit --close) does more than report: its orphan pass auto-heals the model. It converts body-only parent links into native ones, strips the retired labels, moves a now-public repository's self-homed queue items under .github, and attaches every orphan to its home's intake epic. It never closes an item, and it stops loudly — never silently skipping — when a queue is too full to accept more.

After the orphan pass, the sweep runs a security-records pass over the private draft advisories in the org's .github. Each advisory follows the neutral security issues it tracks — closed once every one of them is closed, a draft while any is open — and broken pairs are reported for a human to resolve, never repaired. See vergil-tooling's Security Records guide.

When a finite epic is found outside its home, relocate it: move the issue into .github with vrg-gh issue transfer, then re-establish its task links with vrg-epic-link.

The exact rules and commands are in vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards and its Epic home visibility flips guide.

docs.title: Intake, planning & deferred
docs.text:
The formal path — brainstorm, spec, epic, tasks — is the preferred on-ramp, but most work does not arrive that way. It arrives as a dog-walk epiphany, a "we should probably…", an "oh, don't forget." Intake is the lossless net: it turns raw input into a tracked issue with near-zero friction, so nothing is lost before it can be planned.

Capturing the seed of an idea when it is fresh is more valuable than planning it out on the spot. Intake optimizes for that.

docs.title: Every issue belongs to an epic
docs.text:
The net is not an exception to the model — it is part of it. In every managed repository, every issue is either a legitimate top-level kind (an epic, a per-quarter archive bucket, or a release tracking issue) or has an epic parent. There is no opt-out and no "unlinked" state, and that includes a half-formed idea captured thirty seconds ago.

What makes that workable is that the parent is the state. An issue's parent epic says where it stands, so no label has to restate it:

State Parent Buildable? Intake — captured, not yet reviewed the intake epic no Planning — judged to need a full epic the planning epic no Deferred — evaluated, but waiting on something before it can move the deferred epic no Ready — a one-off, or part of a planned initiative a repository's ad-hoc epic, or a finite epic yes

Work moves intake → planning → ready. An item that has been evaluated but cannot move yet — it waits on an upstream release, another issue, a date, or capacity — steps aside into the deferred queue until its revival conditions are met. Only ready work can be built: the pull-request tooling refuses an issue that still sits in the intake, planning or deferred queue, and says which step to take first.

docs.title: The standing queues
docs.text:
The three queues are standing epics — perpetual, like a repository's ad-hoc epic: created once, reused, never auto-closed. Epic (intake): <name> holds captured, unreviewed items; Epic (planning): <name> holds items waiting for (or undergoing) epic creation; Epic (deferred): <name> holds evaluated items parked until their revival conditions are met.

There is one set per queue home. Every public repository shares the org's set in .github, so the whole org-wide queue is one view rather than something scattered across repositories. A private repository keeps its own set, so private work never surfaces in a public issue. Closed items drain into per-quarter archive buckets, so the live queues show only open work.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Capture. The moment something is worth remembering, it becomes an intake item — filed already linked under the intake epic. A one-line "don't forget X" is valid, and there is no category to choose: a bug, a spark, and an investigation all enter the same way. No planning, no scoping; that is deliberately deferred.
  2. Review. On a periodic pass, intake is reviewed oldest first, in small batches. For each item the agent checks its current state and recommends a route; the human confirms the batch. There are five routes:
  3. Drop — close it with a reason (not planned). It stays searchable.
  4. Defer — move it into the deferred queue, recording why it waits and what to check before it can come back.
  5. One-off — move it into its target repository as a ready task under that repository's ad-hoc epic (or a named epic).
  6. Split — replace it with several ready tasks and close it.
  7. Planning — it needs a real design, so it moves to the planning queue.
  8. Plan. A planning review ranks the planning queue by priority and importance and picks only what will be implemented soon, since a plan left sitting goes stale; each item is picked, deferred, dropped, or left. A planning item is the record of its own epic creation: epic-create always works through one, and leaves progress comments so a session can pause and resume days later. A planning item is waiting, in progress, or completed — closed as "planned as" the epic it became, or with the reason it is not worth doing.
  9. Revisit. A deferred item is never forgotten, because every deferral records a reason and the conditions to check (Revisit when:). On a periodic deferred review, the agent actually checks each item's conditions against their real sources — a release page, an issue's state, a date — and recommends one outcome: keep it (not yet), refresh its record, revive it (back to intake, to planning, or as a one-off), or drop it. Only an item in a queue or an ad-hoc epic can be deferred; a task in a finite epic cannot, since parking one task would in effect suspend its whole epic.

A security item — the neutral issue half of a security record — is routed like any other and keeps its advisory links through every move: every advisory it names is retargeted when the item is transferred or recreated, and its one advisory is retargeted when it is split. A split of an item naming several advisories is refused, since which advisory goes to which task can't be inferred; retarget each by hand with vrg-security-record retarget, then split. See vergil-tooling's Security Records guide.

The intake and planning queues are meant to stay drained: a growing one is a signal to review it, not a place for work to live. The deferred queue is not drained but re-checked — an item stays there exactly as long as its revival conditions are unmet.

docs.title: Nothing escapes
docs.text:
Issues created outside the sanctioned tools — in the web UI, by a script — are healed, not rejected. A daily sweep attaches every orphan it finds to its home's intake epic, so it surfaces at the next review instead of drifting unseen. Placement stays the reviewer's job; the sweep only guarantees that nothing is lost.

The former triage / idea / research kind labels are retired — the parent carries the state now, and the sweep strips the old labels.

docs.title: Visibility changes go one way
docs.text: Because a private repository keeps its own queues and epics, a repository's visibility decides where its work is tracked. Private → public is supported: the sweep moves the repository's open queue items under the org's .github queues, and its epics are relocated to match. Public → private is not supported — work already tracked in public cannot be made private again, so the path is to create a new private repository and migrate the code into it. The audit reports private-repository issues found under public epics for a human to resolve.

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text: The commands and their exact behavior — vrg-intake-create, vrg-intake-route, vrg-queue, the deferral record, the orphan pass, and the queue-home rules — are documented in vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards (see The deferred queue for deferring and reviving) and Epic home visibility flips guide.

docs.title: Tools & skills
docs.text:
The Management layer is operated through two surfaces:

  • vrg-* command-line tools — the mechanical operations (create an epic, link a task, run the audit), maintained in vergil-tooling.
  • Skills — the agent-facing workflows that compose those tools into a process (orchestrate an epic, capture intake, review the queue), maintained in the Claude Code plugin, vergil-claude-plugin.

This page explains how they fit together and who drives what. The dry, per-command reference — every flag of every tool — lives in the repositories where the code does; this is the story, not the man page. For the issue model's mechanics, see vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards.

docs.title: Who drives what
docs.text:
The dividing line is accountability. The speed limit is human comprehension, not code generation — so agents do the development, and humans own the irreversible, outward-facing steps.

Driven by the agent (runs as the user identity) Driven by the human Participating in the brainstorm; running the design-review rounds The judgment calls in the brainstorm, and the decision on each design-review finding and each further round Authoring specs and plans; implementing tasks Submitting the pull request (vrg-submit-pr) Commits and PR preparation / hand-off Reviewing and merging Read-only audits and dry-runs Post-merge finalize (vrg-finalize-pr) Filing intake, epics, tasks, links Write-gated ops: migration --apply, audit --close Implementing a dependency-update fix task Releases (vrg-release) and dependency updates (vrg-update-deps)

An agent never merges and never opens a PR itself: it prepares the change and hands off, and a human takes it across the line.

docs.title: Authoring & structure
docs.text:
• vrg-epic-create (mint an epic in .github)
  • vrg-adhoc-epic (ensure a repo's ad-hoc epic exists)
  • vrg-issue-create (create a task, born linked under an epic)

  • vrg-epic-link / vrg-epic-move / vrg-epic-unlink (manage the epic↔task relationship)

  • vrg-issue-create --epic adhoc|intake|planning (target a repository's standing epic by name rather than by number)

docs.title: Intake, planning & deferred
docs.text:
• vrg-intake-create (capture an intake item, linked under its home's intake epic as it is created — no category to choose)
  • vrg-intake-route (apply a review's route: drop, defer, one-off, split, or planning out of intake; defer or drop out of planning; and out of deferred, revive to intake, planning or one-off, refresh, drop, or split. Defer requires --reason and --revisit-when, and is the only way into or out of the deferred queue. A security item keeps its advisory links when it is transferred, recreated, or split; a split of an item naming several advisories is refused)
  • vrg-queue intake|planning|deferred (the read-only view of one queue — intake oldest first, deferred least recently deferred first — or of all three with a bare vrg-queue; a planning item that any security advisory still tracks is held at in-progress until each advisory it names is retargeted to the task or tasks that fix it)
  • vrg-security-record (record a security finding as a private draft advisory in <org>/.github, paired with a neutral security-labelled intake issue; create, list, show, retarget — see vergil-tooling's Security Records guide)

An issue still in the intake, planning or deferred queue is not buildable: vrg-pr-workflow report-ready and vrg-submit-pr refuse it until it is routed out.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• vrg-epic-rollup (close a finite epic when its last task closes — event-driven)
  • vrg-finalize-pr (merge + post-merge cleanup — human)

docs.title: Reporting & enforcement
docs.text:
• vrg-roadmap (the open-epic roadmap)
  • vrg-epic-audit (drift and invariant violations — read-only, with a gated --close; under --close, run daily by the scheduled sweep, it also runs the orphan pass that attaches every unparented issue to its home's intake epic, then the security-records pass that syncs each advisory's state to its issues and reports broken pairs)
  • vrg-adhoc-migrate (the one-time relocation of the legacy standing epics — complete; the standing alias is retired, so ad-hoc is the only perpetual variant)

To relocate a finite epic into its correct home (.github), move the issue with vrg-gh issue transfer and re-link its tasks with vrg-epic-link.

docs.title: Pull-request flow
docs.text:
• vrg-commit (standards-compliant commits)
  • vrg-pr-workflow report-ready (records the PR hand-off)
  • vrg-submit-pr (open the PR — human-run)

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
• vrg-release (cut a release from develop to main — human-run)
  • vrg-update-deps (the mechanized dependency update — human-run)

A release ends with an update-deps stage, which runs vrg-update-deps once the release is tagged and published. When anything changed, it opens a deps/update-<next> pull request labelled dependency-update, and a green one is merged. If validation or the merge fails, the PR stays open and a fix task is filed. If an updater itself fails, nothing is pushed and the failure is recorded on the release's tracking issue. Any open dependency-update PR blocks the next release, until its fix task closes as completed — the next vrg-release then closes the PR and the gate clears. Two flags change this: --allow-pending-deps lets an urgent release through despite an open PR, and the bypass is logged on the release's tracking issue; --without-deps skips the update-deps stage. The release procedure itself is in vergil-tooling's Releasing guide.

The vrg-gh and vrg-git wrappers sit under all of this, enforcing the allow-lists and selecting the right identity; raw git/gh are blocked in agent sessions.

docs.title: The skills, by role
docs.text:
• epic-create — the outer orchestrator of the workflow: brainstorm → epic → spec → spec pushback rounds → plan → plan pushback rounds → alignment rounds → docs PR → file tasks, always worked through a planning item that records its progress.
  • intake-capture — the lossless net: file an intake item with near-zero friction.
  • intake-review — the periodic pass that reviews the intake queue oldest first, in small batches, and routes each item out of it: drop, defer, one-off, split, or planning.
  • planning-review — ranks the planning queue with the human by priority and importance, hands the item(s) to plan next to epic-create, and defers, drops, or leaves the rest.
  • deferred-review — the periodic pass over the deferred queue: it checks each item's Revisit when: conditions against their real sources and recommends keep, refresh, revive, or drop.
  • migrate-repo — onboard a repository's pre-framework backlog into the epic/task model.
  • issue-implement — the agent implements a single issue end-to-end, runs the advisory agentic-review gate (paad review doctrine), and hands the PR off.
  • pr-watch — the agent monitors an open PR through CI and review, reconciling until it is mergeable.

Together, the tools give the mechanical guarantees and the skills give the process on top of them — which is exactly why the story belongs here, in one place, while each tool's and action's mechanical detail stays in its own repo.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: Getting an idea into shipped, closed tasks is a pipeline — and the whole bet is that front-loading the analysis makes the implementation near-bulletproof. Hours spent up front on design and planning pay for themselves when the pull requests just work the first time.

docs.title: epic-create is the entry point
docs.text:
For non-trivial work, the starting move is epic-create, not brainstorming directly. A solution worth thinking through is worth recording as work, so there is little value in designing something and then walking away from it untracked. epic-create opens into brainstorming and orchestrates the whole sequence. If the design collapses to a trivial, single-PR change, it is a task, not an epic — filed under the target repository's ad-hoc epic, and done.

Every run is tracked in a planning item — an issue in the planning queue that records its own epic creation, with progress comments so a session can pause and resume days later:

  • epic-create <issue> starts or resumes that planning item (an intake or deferred item is first moved to the planning queue).
  • epic-create with a free-text idea first turns the idea into a new planning item.
  • epic-create with no argument summarizes the planning queue and asks which item to work on.

Which item to plan next is decided in planning-review: the human ranks the planning queue by priority and importance and picks only what will be implemented soon, since a plan left sitting goes stale.

The planning item closes once the epic exists, its docs task has merged, and its tasks are filed — "planned as" the epic it became.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
epic-create drives these stages in order:

  1. Brainstorm — explore intent and converge on an approved design.
  2. Initialize — create the epic in .github and seed its bookend tasks (documentation first; documentation review and the retrospective last).
  3. Spec → spec pushback rounds → human review — write the spec, critique it adversarially in spec pushback rounds, and have a human review it.
  4. Plan → plan pushback rounds → alignment rounds — write the implementation plan in one automated pass, critique it in plan pushback rounds, then reconcile the spec and the plan in alignment rounds, which may change both.
  5. Docs PR — land the spec and plan as a single documentation PR (which closes the documentation bookend).
  6. File tasks — create the implementation tasks from the plan, each in the repository where its PR will land.

The review steps in stages 3 and 4 run in human-gated rounds, described below.

docs.title: The interaction doctrine
docs.text:
The design and review steps are not hand-waving — each runs a concrete, reusable skill, composed from two packages: Superpowers (brainstorming, writing-plans) and PAAD (pushback, alignment). Brainstorming produces the spec, pushback critiques the spec, writing-plans generates the plan, pushback critiques the plan, and alignment confirms the spec and the plan match. The pipeline mixes interactive, human-gated and automated stages on purpose:

Stage Mode Contract superpowers:brainstorming interactive Explore intent, one question at a time — produces the spec. Design review (pushback on the spec, pushback on the plan, alignment) human-gated rounds A fresh review-only subagent per round. The main session walks the human through the findings, and the human decides every further round. superpowers:writing-plans automated Generate the implementation plan in one pass; no gating.

Each design-review round reviews the whole document, and the main session records it as a comment on the planning item. The human decides every finding and whether to run another round of the stage. The rules are in the paad review doctrine, mode 1. How the workflow uses PAAD, and every place it deviates from the PAAD authors' recommendations, is recorded in the paad usage policy.

The human-judgment principle governs brainstorming: stop and ask only for ambiguities or judgment calls that materially affect the outcome; handle minor, obvious corrections by batching them to the end as a single "here are the no-brainers — correct me if I'm wrong" review, rather than gating each one.

Design review walks the findings one at a time, in severity order, except for one batch at the end: low findings, each with its own decision, and known findings, which keep their earlier decision unless the human pulls one out (doctrine §2.2, step 4).

The goal of all this front-loading is blunt: plans that just work — on the order of 90–99% of tasks green on first implementation. Real-world misses still happen and get patched, but the more upfront refinement, the higher the success rate, and the more mechanical work can eventually be forked off and trusted to run on its own.

Each task is then implemented with the issue-implement skill, which runs an agentic-review gate before it hands the PR off. The gate is advisory: when it pauses, the human can accept the branch as it stands. The rules are in the paad review doctrine.
